brief: TS Lombard argues Fed chair Warsh, working with Treasury Secretary Bessent, faces two paths: hike the funds rate and invert the curve, which the author calls symbolic but ultimately ineffective, or hold the short end and let the long end rise, resetting risk preferences. The author expects Warsh to use Friday's CPI print to justify avoiding a September hike and instead let the curve steepen; if Warsh hikes anyway, the historical trade of buying 30-year Treasuries and selling 10-year Treasuries may not work this time. The underlying case: private-sector debt is a shrinking share of total debt growth while Federal borrowing, insensitive to rates, keeps expanding, so since 2012 inflation has correlated more with growth in Federal debt (6-quarter lag) than private debt (4-quarter lag), reversing the pre-2012 pattern. Because the private sector is now less leveraged and less rate-sensitive, an inverted 3-month/10-year curve takes longer to cause recession; the last inversion ran 25 months without ever triggering one. The route the author sees Bessent and Warsh possibly pursuing: hold the funds rate, let Treasury borrow cheaply short-term, and let the market push 10-year yields higher to clear supply and demand.

cards.claim: TS Lombard says raising the funds rate to invert the yield curve would be symbolic but ultimately ineffective.
cards.anchor: Raise the funds rate & invert the curve! Symbolic but ultimately ineffective.

cards.claim: Warsh and Bessent are considering holding the funds rate at the short end while letting long-term yields rise to reset risk preferences.
cards.anchor: Hold the short end, let the long end rise, and allow risk preferences to reset

cards.claim: TS Lombard expects Warsh to use the CPI data to avoid a September rate hike and instead let the yield curve steepen.
cards.anchor: I still think Warsh finds a way through the CPI data to avert a Sep hike and lets the curve steepen

cards.claim: If the Fed hikes, the historical trade has been to buy 30-year Treasuries and sell 10-year Treasuries, though TS Lombard suggests this time may differ.
cards.anchor: Hiking means buying 30s and selling 10s, this time may be different.

cards.claim: Friday's CPI report will be scrutinized for a rationale to let Warsh avoid a rate hike.
cards.anchor: CPI on Friday will be dissected to find a way for Warsh to keep from hiking.

cards.claim: The most recent yield curve inversion lasted 25 months and never triggered a recession.
cards.anchor: The last inversion (25 months!) never even flipped the economy (close, but no cigar).
cards.topic: Private vs Federal debt driving inflation

cards.claim: Since 2012, growth in Federal government debt has correlated with inflation more strongly, with a 6-quarter lag, than household and nonfinancial business debt.
cards.anchor: growth in Federal debt has had a larger, more significant correlation with inflation (6Q lag) since 2012 than household and nonfinancial business debt
cards.topic: Private vs Federal debt driving inflation

cards.claim: The ratio of credit card debt outstanding to retail sales excluding motor vehicles has not returned to pre-GFC levels, and its small post-Covid bounce has reversed.
cards.anchor: The ratio has not returned to pre-GFC levels and, with the surge in interest rate charges, the small post-Covid bounce has reversed.

cards.claim: Household margin debt used to buy equities has soared in absolute terms but, scaled to equity market values, remains below pre-Covid levels.
cards.anchor: while leverage has soared, its rise is in line with equity market values and, against that scalar, still not back to pre-Covid levels

cards.claim: Since the start of the year, the 10-year yield 10 years forward has narrowed to the spot 10-year yield, possibly anticipating rate hikes.
cards.anchor: since the year began, perhaps in anticipation of eventual rate hikes, the 10Y yield 10Y forward has narrowed to the spot yield

cards.claim: TS Lombard expects to fade the typical pattern of the forward-spot spread reversing once the Fed starts hiking, believing it will not hold this time.
cards.anchor: This time around, I am not convinced. Initially that will be the market reaction, but I would fade the move.

cards.claim: The US sends about 3% of US GDP abroad to increase the global supply of dollars, and there is currently no alternative destination large enough to absorb a redirection of that capital.
cards.anchor: at least not in the size to absorb the 3% of US GDP that the US sends to increase the global supply of dollars.
